summary: This standards-track document defines a Lightweight DHCPv6 Relay Agent that adds relay options identifying the client-facing interface. It can run on access devices such as DSLAMs and Ethernet switches that do not do IPv6 routing. That lets the DHCPv6 server know which port a request came from.

plainLanguage.summary: A small helper at a building's mail room stamps each request with which door it came from. The server then knows who is asking.

subtitle: How a plain Layer 2 switch can tag DHCPv6 requests with the port they came from, without being a router.

tldr.problem: On a bridged access network with many nodes on one link, a DHCPv6 server or relay agent normally cannot tell how a client is attached to the network.
tldr.mechanism: A Lightweight DHCPv6 Relay Agent (LDRA) in the access node wraps each client message in a Relay-Forward message that carries an Interface-ID option naming the client-facing interface, with no routing or IPv6 control functions.
tldr.outcome: Servers can use the Interface-ID to identify clients and apply assignment policies. RFC 6221 is a Standards Track document that updates RFC 3315 and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 6221 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2011 that updates RFC 3315, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Lightweight Relay Agent
sections.content:
A normal DHCPv6 relay agent, as defined in RFC 3315, forwards messages between clients and servers that are not on the same IPv6 link. It is usually built into a router.

The Lightweight DHCPv6 Relay Agent (LDRA) is for access nodes that only bridge at the link layer, such as Digital Subscriber Link Access Multiplexers (DSLAMs) and Ethernet switches. An LDRA sits on the same IPv6 link as the client and as a DHCPv6 relay agent or server. It does not implement IPv6 control functions such as ICMPv6, and it has no routing capability.

The RFC says it is functionally the equivalent of the Layer 2 Relay Agent proposed for DHCPv4. It also notes a typical use in a broadband service provider network.
sections.plainLanguage: Some network boxes only pass traffic along and are not smart enough to be routers. This document lets even those simple boxes add a little note to each request.

sections.title: The Problem on Aggregation Networks
sections.content:
Many access networks aggregate IPv6 nodes into one or more routers using IEEE 802.1D bridging or something similar. Many nodes share a single link, so a DHCPv6 server or relay agent would normally be unaware of how a given client is attached.

The LDRA fixes that by inserting Relay Agent Information, including the Interface-ID option from RFC 3315, so the server can use it to identify the client.

The document defines a few terms. A client-facing interface carries traffic towards the DHCPv6 client. A network-facing interface carries traffic towards the DHCPv6 server or servers. The access node combines many interfaces onto one link and is not IP-aware in the data path.
sections.plainLanguage: When lots of computers share one wire, the server cannot tell which plug each one is in. The LDRA writes down the plug number for it.

sections.title: Message Formats and Mandatory Options
sections.content:
The LDRA does not invent new messages. To stay interoperable with existing relays and servers, the message format is unchanged from RFC 3315, and the LDRA uses the same two relay message types: Relay-Forward and Relay-Reply.

In a Relay-Forward message built by an LDRA, the link-address MUST be the unspecified address, the peer-address is set as described in the agent behaviour, and the Interface-ID option MUST be included. The LDRA MAY add other relay agent options.

Every Relay-Forward message from an LDRA MUST carry two options. The Relay-Message option holds the original client DHCP message (the payload without the UDP and IP headers). If the result would exceed the MTU of the outgoing interface, it MUST be discarded and an error condition SHOULD be logged.

The Interface-ID option identifies the client-facing interface. The server MUST include it in a Relay-Reply so the LDRA knows where to send the decapsulated message. Its format is outside the scope of the RFC and it SHOULD be treated as an opaque value, which the server SHOULD NOT try to parse. The LDRA SHOULD use the same value for a given interface and SHOULD retain it across restarts, because a changing value would break server assignment policies.
sections.plainLanguage: The LDRA puts the original request in an envelope and writes the door number on the outside. The reply comes back with the same door number, so the LDRA knows where to deliver it.

sections.title: How the Agent Behaves
sections.content:
Every interface of an LDRA MUST be configured as either client-facing or network-facing.

For client messages, the LDRA MUST intercept all traffic arriving on a client-facing interface that is sent to ff02::1:2 (All_DHCP_Relay_Agents_and_Servers), uses UDP and has destination port 547. It MUST stop the original message from being forwarded on the network-facing interface. It sets link-address to :: and includes the Interface-ID. If the message it received was already a Relay-Forward message, it sets the new hop-count to the received hop-count plus 1. It copies the client's IP source address into the peer-address field, and it copies the destination and source addresses from the client message into the Relay-Forward message.

The LDRA MUST discard client-side messages of type ADVERTISE (2), REPLY (7), RECONFIGURE (10) and RELAY-REPL (13), since a client never sends those. It MUST NOT validate the options inside the message, leaving that to the server so new options can be introduced without changing the LDRA.

For replies, the LDRA intercepts UDP traffic on the network-facing interface with link-local source and destination addresses and destination port 547, and forwards only Relay-Reply messages. The reply is valid if it passes the usual relay checks and the Interface-ID is present and matches a valid interface. The LDRA unwraps the Relay Message option and forwards it to the client, and SHOULD NOT retransmit it on any other interface.
sections.plainLanguage: The LDRA catches every request from a client, wraps it with the door number, and sends it on. When a reply comes back, it unwraps it and hands it only to the right door.

sections.title: Network Topologies
sections.content:
The RFC walks through three layouts and shows what the server would receive for a Solicit message in each.

Client and server on the same link. The access node acts as a bridge and knows nothing about IP prefixes on the link, so the server should treat address and parameter assignment as if the message were not relayed. To support this, DHCP servers conforming to the RFC MUST ignore a link-address value of zero for address selection. This is the change the RFC makes to RFC 3315, Section 11. The server sees a Relay-Forward message with hop-count 0 and the LDRA-inserted interface-id.

Client and server behind another relay agent. The LDRA sends Relay-Forward messages upstream to a second relay agent (RelayB). The server receives an outer Relay-Forward with hop-count 1 that contains the LDRA's Relay-Forward with hop-count 0.

A relay agent in front of the LDRA. An RFC 3315 relay agent (RelayC) sits on the client-facing side. The server receives three nested Relay-Forward messages, with hop-counts 2, 1 and 0, around the original Solicit.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes there is one helper between you and the server, and sometimes there are several. Each helper adds its own envelope, so the server opens the envelopes one by one.

sections.title: Trust and Security
sections.content:
An LDRA MUST have a setting for every client-facing interface that marks it trusted or untrusted, and this SHOULD be configurable per interface. If an interface is untrusted, the LDRA MUST discard any RELAY-FORW (12) message received from it. This stops a client from pretending to be a relay agent.

The security issues of RFC 3315 relay agents also apply to LDRAs. The LDRA SHOULD apply some form of rate-limiting on client-originated traffic to prevent excessive processing load. It can identify the traffic easily, since it only listens to client traffic sent to the DHCP servers and relay agents address on UDP port 547. Messages above the rate limit may be silently discarded.

The RFC also warns that hop-count-based judgement of whether an LDRA can be trusted can easily be defeated by a rogue relay agent on the network-facing interface.
sections.plainLanguage: The LDRA should not believe a plug that claims to be a helper, and it should not get swamped if someone sends too many requests. Even so, a fake helper on the server side of the box could still fool it.
